title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Summary

Speech acts: utterances that use a particular locution with a conventional meaning to achieve a certain social effect.
Conversational implicatures: inferences tied to particular speech acts, based on:

general principles of rational, cooperative communication (Grice 1975);
conventional meanings.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Where do we go next?

→ conventional meaning



First, we need to develop methods for observing and classifying inference types.
Then, we can focus on the conventional stuff:

study how it is encoded in linguistic expressions.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Defining inference
What is an inference?

A relation between expressions of a language.

\(E_{1} ↝ E_{2}\)

Typically, \(E_{2}\) is a declarative sentence.




Jo did some of the readings.  ↝ Jo didn’t do all of the readings.
Could you bring the dog inside?  ↝ There is a dog.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Data collection
Where do inferences come from?

Speakers of the language!

Your friends.
Laboratory experiments.
Large crowd-sourced inference judgment studies.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
This class
Semantics is the study of conventional meaning in natural language.

Goal: give a ridiculously precise account of the inferences that linguistic expressions trigger.
If we can do this, then we have captured what these expressions mean\(_{NN}\).

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
A taxonomy of inference types

Some types of inference observable in natural language:

entailment
conversational implicature
presupposition
conventional implicature

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Entailment

A relationship between declarative sentences.
If \(S_{1}\) entails \(S_{2}\), then whenever \(S_{1}\) is true, \(S_{2}\) must be true.

Jo has at least three siblings.  ↝ Jo has at least two siblings.

Entailments are non-defeasible.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Non-defeasibility of entailments

#Jo has at least three siblings, {and, but} she doesn’t have at least two siblings.
# Jo is Bo’s sibling, {and, but} Jo and Bo aren’t siblings.
#No one came to class, {and, but} it’s not the case that Julian didn’t come to class.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Conversational implicature

Typically a relationship between utterances of declarative sentences.
If an utterance of \(S_{1}\) conversationally implicates \(S_{2}\), then the utterance means\(_{NN}\) \(S_{2}\).
Conversational implicatures are defeasible.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Defeasibility of conversational implicatures

Jo did some of the readings. In fact, she did all of them.
I want something with lots of caffeine. In fact, I want a matcha latte.
Context: Jo is writing a letter of rec. for Bo for the ling. instructor position.  Jo: Bo is very punctual. He has great handwriting. Last, but not least, he’d be a great ling. instructor!

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Presupposition

A relationship between an expression and a declarative sentence.
If \(E\) presupposes \(S\), then whenever an utterance of \(E\) is felicitous, \(S\) is true.

Jo stopped smoking.  ↝ Jo used to smoke.

Presuppositions are non-defeasible.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Non-defeasibility of presuppositions

#Jo stopped smoking, {and, but} she didn’t used to smoke.
#Jo loves that it’s raining, {and, but} it’s not raining.
#Bo failed the assignment, {and, but} there isn’t an assignment.
#Bo failed the assignment again, {and, but} he hasn’t failed it before.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Things to address

Difference between entailment and presupposition.
Conventional implicature versus the other inference types.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Entailment vs. presupposition
First pass:

Presuppositions encode background information, needed to make sense of some expression.

Express what must already be in the common ground (Stalnaker 1978).

Entailments encode information about what is said.

Express information, e.g., which is being added to the common ground.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
The negation test
Second pass:

Presuppositions project, whereas entailments do not.



Jo demonstrated that she’s good at Go. 
Jo loves that she’s good at Go.


Jo didn’t demonstrate that she’s good at Go. 
Jo doesn’t love that she’s good at Go.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
More!


Bo brought a dog to his place of work. 
Bo brought the dog to his place of work.


Bo didn’t bring a dog to his place of work. 
Bo didn’t bring the dog to his place of work.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
The question test


Did Jo demonstrate that she’s good at Go?
Does Jo love that she’s good at Go?


Did Jo bring a dog to his place of work? 
Did Jo bring the dog to his place of work?

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
The conditional test


If Jo demonstrated that she’s good at Go, she’ll have to join the Go league. 
If Jo loves that she’s good at Go, she’ll have to join the Go league.


If Bo brought a dog to his place of work, the boss will be mad. 
If Bo brought the dog to his place of work, the boss will be mad.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Families of sentences
These tests are known as family-of-sentence tests (Chierchia and McConnell-Ginet 1990).

Given a sentence \(S_{1}\), from which you can infer \(S_{2}\):

negate \(S_{1}\);
question \(S_{1}\);
put \(S_{1}\) into the antecedent of a conditional.



If \(S_{2}\) survives (i.e., projects), probably a presupposition.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Hey, wait a minute!
The hey, wait a minute test (Fintel 2004).

Bo: You love that you’re good at Go.  Jo: Hey, wait a minute! I’m not good at Go!
Bo: You demonstrated that you’re good at Go!  Jo: #Hey, wait a minute! I’m not good at Go!  Jo: No, I didn’t!

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Hey, wait a minute!

Jo: You brought the dog to your place of work!  Bo: Hey, wait a minute! There isn’t a dog!

Distinguishing entailments and presuppositions from conversational implicatures:

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Now you try it!

Mo forgot that he went to class.  ↝ Mo went to class.



Mo forgot to eat breakfast.  ↝ Mo didn’t eat breakfast.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Question

Why do presuppositions “project”?

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Disappearing presuppositions

If Bo has a dog, he brought the dog to his place of work.
If Jo is actually good at Go, she loves that she’s good at Go.



It’s not true that Bo has a dog and that he brought the dog to his place of work.
It’s not true that Jo is good at Go and that she loves that she’s good at Go.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Changing presuppositions

If Jo has any friends in Gainesville, she loves that she gets to see them.  ↝ If Jo has any friends in Gainesville, she gets to see them.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Conventional implicatures

The class is taught by Julian, who enjoys syntax.  ↝ Julian enjoys syntax.
The class isn’t taught by Julian, who enjoys syntax.  ↝ Julian enjoys syntax.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Can they disappear?

#If Julian enjoys syntax, then the class is taught by Julian, who enjoys syntax.
